items.explain: They may attend a booked chest X-ray this week, though they missed a previous follow-up appointment.
The person's scans and tests show a probable lung infection, likely tuberculosis, and supervised treatment begins.
Because of the illness, the person gets priority for a shelter bed during treatment, but only when one is free.
After losing the shelter bed and contact point, the person skips some treatment doses.
The person reclaims jobseeker benefits using the clinic or shelter as an address; the old job no longer exists.
The person returns to sleeping on the streets, repeatedly moved on, living on cash from a market.
The person dies after long breathing decline worsened by exposure to cold, on or near the streets.
The person is expected to die of lung failure or pneumonia in 2059, aged 53.
Using the library as an address, the person can finally get repeat blood pressure prescriptions from a clinic.

items.plain: Sleeps under a bridge in winter
items.explain: The shelter is full in winter, so the person often sleeps in an underpass in the cold.
A young volunteer who supported the person moves away for university, weakening that connection.
The person's social housing application doesn't move up, so they rely on the library and shelters.
The person may have a stroke from high blood pressure; medication lowers but doesn't remove the risk.
The person catches a chest infection from the cold and goes to hospital with no home to return to.
The person dies one winter while still homeless, with the housing application never resolved.
The person is expected to die of pneumonia after cold exposure in 2058, aged 73.
Children's services start assessing the family's care of a child, while benefit cuts are paused.
The person and a neighbour formally complain to the council about mould in the home.
The person's child goes to hospital with a severe asthma attack caused by the damp home.

items.plain: Loses work hours at care job
items.explain: The person's care work hours drop too low, forcing a second insecure job, with unpaid travel cutting income.
The person joins a local tenants' group, and the mould problem becomes part of its campaign.
Social services impose a child protection plan citing the home's conditions, damp and neighbour complaints.

items.plain: Develops chronic heart or lung disease
items.explain: In middle age the person is diagnosed with long-term heart or lung illness linked to poverty and damp.
The person is expected to die of heart disease in 2091, aged 69.
Rejecting offered concessions, the person protests outside the council building with a neighbour without permission.
The person becomes a regular named organiser of a small, formal tenants' group around building complaints.
The person withholds service charges as protest; the council treats it as debt and starts eviction proceedings.
The person never returns to paid work in their mid-fifties and lives on long-term benefits.
The person is transferred to a different social housing flat, weakening their local organising.
The person likely develops long-term heart or metabolic illness from years of sitting, stress and stairs.
The person is expected to die of a heart or circulation problem in 2070, aged 71.
The person doesn't show up for an arranged job placement, spending the time with an older acquaintance instead.
The person keeps earning cash through an informal crew, though an older acquaintance warns them off.
The person is arrested again for theft-like offences linked to needing cash.
The person gets a second conviction and a short prison sentence, losing their rented room.
The person leaves prison with nowhere to live, sleeps under a bridge, and struggles to find work.
In a less likely path, the person leaves the city for warehouse work elsewhere.
The person drifts between cash jobs, petty crime and shelters while their health steadily worsens.
The person is expected to die of a drug overdose in 2071, aged 40.
The person keeps cutting methadone to quit fully to see a grandchild, lowering drug tolerance without naloxone.
The person is repeatedly stopped by police and likely held, possibly arrested.
The person gets more supervised visits with a daughter and grandson, as long as drug tests stay clean.
The person's casual scrapyard income shrinks and volunteering is blocked, leaving little structure to days.
After a setback, the person starts using opioids again while their tolerance is dangerously low.
The person dies of an opioid overdose alone at home, with no overdose antidote nearby.
The person is expected to die of an opioid overdose in 2057, aged 63.
The person takes a same-level job with a pay bump, overseeing automation that will cut 44 jobs.
The person's child leaves for university, leaving a strained two-adult household and less contact.
The person might sell the house and leave town for a job, though this is made less likely.

items.plain: Diagnosed with high blood pressure, drinking
items.explain: The person's heavier drinking and insomnia lead to diagnoses of high blood pressure and harmful drinking.
The person's management job is cut by automation, and they find lower-paid work locally.
After separating, the person sells or remortgages the house and rents somewhere smaller in town.
The person has a stroke caused by years of uncontrolled blood pressure and drinking.
The person is expected to die of a bleeding stroke in 2077, aged 65.
The person does final soup kitchen shifts before leaving, staying in touch with a homeless friend.
The person's part-time barista job ends before moving away.
The person moves to another city to study social work, with a parent paying.
The person's parents split up, and contact narrows mostly to one parent.
The person finishes a social work degree.
The person applies for a housing casework job back home but is steered away from housing decisions.
The person stays involved in tenant and housing advocacy, location uncertain.
The person dies in old age of a heart-related cause.
The person goes to the clinic with a neighbour and picks up lapsed antidepressants in person.
The person sees neighbours less, relying mainly on one neighbour who is under strain himself.
The person changes their will without a lawyer, as if putting affairs in order before death.
The person may stop antidepressants and refuse help, though deliveries and visits make this less likely.
Living alone, the person falls or gets ill, isn't found for days, and goes to hospital.
After hospital, the person likely refuses supported housing or moving abroad near their son.

items.plain: Dies of frailty and heart failure
items.explain: The person is expected to die of frailty and heart failure in 2055, aged 86.
The person's partner privately reveals some of a secret data deal between an employer and the council.
The person compiles notes into a public account of predictive surveillance, while officials give empty replies.
The person's engagement ends; they move out and rent alone nearby.
The person's employer reviews their computer use, likely leading to a warning or reassignment.
The person leaves for a city beyond the system's surveillance, having already prepared.
The person likely builds a career defending public access to records elsewhere.
The person dies at 81 of a common cause, guessed from population averages.
The person is expected to die of heart disease in 2098, aged 81.
The person completes an automation project that eliminates 44 jobs on schedule.
The person's engagement ends over secrets they can't share, and they move out.
The person survives job cuts and is given more forecasting responsibility.
The person signs a renewed data-sharing deal, taking on deeper secrecy obligations.
The person buys a home, likely in a nicer neighbourhood.
The person is promoted to a regional role and moves away, still overseeing the data deal.
The person likely develops high blood pressure from years of high-pressure work.
The person is expected to die of a heart attack in 2091, aged 76.
